text: distracted?" "What?" He blinked at me. "Could we distract it—draw its attention toward us and away from the ship—and then slip out of its grip—" Arlysa shook her head violently. "What could we do that wouldn't seem puny to it?" Her voice was bitter and despairing. What grip did this thing have on her? "Is it aware of our thoughts—our feelings?" I asked, groping. "Aware, but doesn't understand yet," said Rueldo. "Well—can we trick it? Confuse it somehow?" Rueldo snorted. "An opportunity like this—that anyone with a soul would kill for—and you can't wait to escape!" "Yes!" I shouted. "Do you want to die for that thing out there—?" "It's the spirit that matters!" Rueldo cried. "Reach out to it with your heart—with your soul!" The deck shuddered again. Frost crystals glittered on metal surfaces. Outside a great glowing eye peered in at us. The spirit? I wondered. The heart? I stared out at the luminous thing that held us prisoner, and the idea I'd dismissed as absurd came back in a rush. It was outlandish, I knew that . . . and perhaps it was ridiculous . . . but perhaps Arlysa would see what I meant, would understand . . . would agree . . . . Before I could utter a word, Arlysa retorted to Rueldo, "What are we supposed to do—make love to it?" She gestured contemptuously. There was a trace of spirit, yet, beneath her despair. I took a breath and struggled to keep my voice even. "Maybe not. Maybe we're to make love to each other." She wheeled. "You're as mad as he is!" "Am I?" I croaked. Perhaps I was. We were trapped by a creature so alien I scarcely knew what it was—only that its very existence endangered our lives—and here I was suggesting that we show it the extent of the human heart, that we create right here in its presence the act that symbolized the greatest intensity of the human spirit. I proposed no mere act of coupling, but the true joining and bounding of love. Could Arlysa find those feelings in herself? Would she want to? Would I? "Arlysa." I took a halting step toward her. "We might turn it from destroying us." She looked at me oddly, her face illuminated by the glow of the quasar creature. Perhaps the creature itself sensed something of the invisible sparks shooting between us, because a stronger radiance suddenly fell across Arlysa's face. I looked out to see a luminous iris now surrounding the eyelike structure. "Do it!" Rueldo roared. He was at the far corner of the bridge, silhouetted against the eerie glow. "Show it the ultimate! Show it love! Let it know the human soul!" His eyes flashed, not at me but at Arlysa. Did he know what he was saying? Was I as mad as he was? I reached out a hand to touch Arlysa. Her eyes were closed, thumbnail pressed to her lip, concentrating on something inside herself. "What do you feel?" I whispered. It was a long moment before she answered. Finally she opened her eyes a crack, and glanced first at Rueldo and then at me. Her eyes betrayed her internal struggle. "Maybe—" she said hoarsely. "It's crazy. But maybe—it would work." A smile cracked her lips, and for an instant I saw the maverick young metaxawoman surface in the sharp eyes, the angular jaw. She laughed. "Besides," she whispered, "if it doesn't work—what better way to go?" My breath went out, and my legs weakened under me. I was dizzy with several kinds of fear, all churning together. "I—I mean—" I gulped, my tongue in knots. I was painfully aware of Rueldo standing behind me, and I wondered what he would feel. Jealousy? Indifference? Did it really matter? I gazed at Arlysa, and saw anger flash back into her eyes. Then the anger transformed itself to amusement, and her jaw was set once more with confidence. This was the metaxawoman I thought I knew, the little girl from Toynbrun grown strong. Her eyes turned to pools surrounded by shadows of pain. She stepped closer to me, and before I knew how to react, she was touching my hair, stroking and entwining her fingers in it. She pulled me to her, and then as our lips came together, there was an electrical sparkle where our lifepack fields intersected and joined. She brushed her lips to mine, and then her breath was warm against my neck as she sighed. Clumsily I pressed her to me and buried my face in her hair. I could feel her trembling and stiffening as one feeling and then another took hold. Through the mistiness of my eyes and the haze of her hair and the sparkle of our interacting fields, I could just see the crimson and gold radiance of the creature that was responsible for our dilemma. Could it sense our fear? Was that what kept it interested? Was there any hope that it would sense our passion, our craving for life—that it would spare us? I felt the force of its presence, watching; but whether it was a benign or evil presence I couldn't tell. I knew only that Arlysa's and my actions, and our emotions, might spell the difference for us between life and death. Could we show this creature the heights reached by the human spirit? I clutched Arlysa to me in hope and terror. * * * Heedless of my interrogators, I held the touchglass to my forehead for nearly a full minute, conscious only of the blinding, soothing music of the light-harps in my brains, sluicing away the memory and the pain. Only when the music so filled me that it taxed the capacity of my head did I lower the crystal and raise my eyes again. Commander Toarn was watching me with a stony stare, his ears fluttering as though being tickled by a breeze. Lieutenant Amygdol was squinting, perhaps wondering if he was being taken in by a cheap bluff. I took a breath to continue, but was interrupted by Toarn's whisper. "This act you speak of . . . it is regarded by your race as . . . as . . ." He fluttered his long fingers, searching for the right word. "Mystical—is it not?" I hesitated, unsure how to answer. That was, of course, precisely the point of Arlysa's and my . . . performance. And yet—even the most casual student of human history knew that through the ages men had often subordinated sexual activity to the status of mere animal pleasure. Come to think of it, though, even as a recreation devoid of bonding, the activity was imbued with an aura of mysticism far outstripping the actual pleasure involved. As I struggled with this question, Lieutenant Amygdol unexpectedly came to my rescue. He chuckled, saying, "I think, Commander, that you've stymied him with a question that human artists have wrestled with for centuries. Humans have never been able to decide whether sex is nothing more than instinct, or is something that belongs in the realms of the mystics and angels." He winked at me. "Right, Mr. Kandrell?" My face reddened. I refrained from pointing out that what I was talking about was not sex per se, but a gestalt of sex and love, which was something else entirely. Amygdol seemed to be trying to help me—and maybe he meant the same thing, anyway. Another historical fact is that it's a rare period in which ordinary humans can talk freely and articulately about this subject. "I see," whispered the pedriquat doubtfully. The lieutenant nodded and sat back. "Now, maybe we can hear how it all came out," he said, winking again. I sighed, deciding that he had apparently not caught the distinction, after all. Nevertheless, the story needed to be told. * * * Sensing my fear, Arlysa found the strength to melt slowly, ever so slowly in my rigid embrace. The warmth of her breath against my skin, the tiny movements of her body, the prolonged, penetrating kiss and the stare of those eyes filled with pain, a sharing pain—all warmed me till I was free of the ice of fear, allowed me to loosen my clutch on her. With a gentle laugh, she drew herself back a few inches and gazed into my eyes. I laughed in a twitchy, self-conscious way, and then allowed myself to smile as I recognized the tenderness that had entered her eyes. We stood that way for a few seconds or perhaps an hour, scarcely mindful of the presence of another life-force around us, simply holding one another and basking in our mutual presence. Whatever terror Arlysa had felt now seemed forgotten or hid away; and I felt the last of my own fears give way in a ripple that spread to my fingertips and toes, and back up my spine. There, in the light of the quasar creature, my desire for Arlysa reawakened; and out of the desire something more powerful was aroused, something that had lain sleeping—a power that wrapped itself around and through the bare desire like a spell entwined through the sinews of a living sword in the old legends, dwarfing and yet transmuting it into a force a thousand times more potent. Was that power love? If not, it was something for which no word has yet been created. Arlysa's hands were working to loosen my jumpsuit. I responded to her evident arousal as I reached to unfasten hers. Whatever the magic was, I was not alone in being transformed by it. Outside the spacecraft, a fabulous sentient being was shimmering and glowing in changing colors as it streamed out of the tortured world of alterspace. A corner of that being's mind was bound up in Arlysa's, and perhaps in mine, as well. Was its power joining with ours? Were emotions that might have lain forever unawakened in my heart, and in Arlysa's, being charged and brought forth in a three-way gestalt, united in both physical and psychic bonding there before the viewport? Our garments cast aside, we were soon clothed only in the sparkle of our interacting lifepack fields. My dragon awakened from his slumber, and Arlysa responded in kind, neither of us much troubled by the shadowy presence of Rueldo—or by the brooding living light staring in from space, perhaps comprehending and perhaps not, but surely not indifferent. We joined and closed with one another, and in Arlysa's eyes and in the movements of her body I felt an acceptance and devotion to me and to our joined spirits, and my heart soared beyond reason or hope. Outside the spaceship, a creature of fantastic tenuousness and size was listening and feeling, perhaps astounded and perhaps stupefied—but understanding, I think, a little. * * * Lights shadowed around us like a waterfall, flashing bright and dark, cascading upon us in rippling colors as though the spaceship were without walls. We were locked in a bewitching, dizzying embrace—and yet my mind was totally clear in the knowledge that I loved Arlysa as I had never thought to love a woman. I searched the depths of those emerald-brown eyes, watched them close with pleasure and pain, and then open again to flicker over my face, reaching, touching, searching within for my soul. There was nothing I would have kept hidden from her; I would have killed for her or walked into death for her, or walked away, if that was what she needed. Even in those moments, a fragment of my mind recognized the strangeness in what was occurring—the light streaming into the ship, streaming out of the very air surrounding us—and the shadowy silhouette of Rueldo, dancing and gesturing before the creature. Then the change started: first, Rueldo's presence touching the edges of our gestalt, a spiritual rather than physical presence. I felt Arlysa responding with surprise and pleasure, and then Rueldo's thoughts not just brushing, but entering the magical zone; and for a moment I was wrenched with jealousy, and then I thought, he could be a part of it, too, it would be a greater union than ever, it was natural, and I'd always wondered if he and Arlysa . . . . . . and that was when it began coming apart. I realized that she was slipping from me, her attention drawing away; something was coming between us. No! I cried, straining to hold her tightly with my mind as with my body. Arlysa! I could hear her calling to me, as though across a gulf of space. The threads of our embrace were unraveling faster than I could follow in my dizziness, and retangling again in another form, a form excluding me. Arlysa and Rueldo were coming together, and I was on the outside, straining to remain a part of her; but that something else was entwining itself around them, the chosen two, the ones who could hear it. Though I still clutched her in my arms, Arlysa was becoming insubstantial, a shimmering sylph—and I was dimly aware of Rueldo, now motionless before the viewport—and of a bizarre, stroboscopic disjointedness in the flow of time . . . . . . and afterwards there was a fragmented, dreamlike memory of a bubbling fountain of light smashing my world and sending me reeling into unconsciousness. Later I awakened, shaking with cold horror and a great emptiness, and a feeling that a part of me had been ripped out of my skull. I was alone on the bridge, clothed only in my lifepack field. The automatic controls flickered with restored life, and my stomach told me that I had just recently come out of alterspace. Exhausted, I sat a while just clutching my sweaty jumpsuit, and Arlysa's. I pressed her suit to my face, trying to stop the damned tears; but they would not stop, and the smell of Arlysa in the cloth only made the emptiness deeper and more hurtful, and I could do nothing except shake and sob with the pain. Eventually I was too exhausted to cry any longer, and I got to my feet and went to the computer asking for answers. What I found, though startling, could scarcely shock me further. Pixikin was entering the interplanetary region of Arxus—the pedriquat system—a good dozen light- years from our previous position. And my shipmates? I wandered the corridors and compartments of the ship, calling quietly, but I knew what I would find. And of course I was right. * * * Commander Toarn, I swear, was weeping. His ears were laid back flat, his nostrils flared—and yet his eyebrows were quivering, and almost inaudibly, he was whispering, "A hero of the people! A true hero!" Lieutenant Amygdol, however, was staring at me with a stolid expression. "You still haven't told us," he said tonelessly, "what became of your companions. For the record." Ah, he knew, then—he just wanted to be told. "I assume they're still out there," I answered, thinking how badly I wanted to just go hole up in a bar somewhere and submerge that memory in a deep pool of intoxication. "Out there—?" I gestured vaguely. "With the creature—wherever." I thought for a moment, thankful that my feelings were bubbling beneath the surface but not pouring out, and I finished in a rush of words. "We succeeded in getting its attention, all right. We showed it human emotion—and in some way I'll never understand, it joined in, made the bond total—and then tore it away from me." I blinked. "Don't you see? It worked too well. The creature fell in love with her, too—or fell in love with love. And so it kept her for itself, her and Rueldo, the two it knew how to touch. It controls space and alterspace, and so it kept them and threw me out." "But it protected you—sent you to a place of safety." I shrugged. Safety? I had lost a love that could not come twice in a lifetime. The lieutenant persisted. "You said she hated the thing." "So maybe she loves it now. Or maybe they're in some kind of Hell together," I grunted. I shifted my gaze to the pedriquat, who was watching me in apparent wonder. "May I go now?" I said softly. "You are a hero of the people," he whispered. "You have proven our ancestor Pomprey famous and right. There must be honors, ceremonies." I shook my head. "Not now. Later, perhaps—" "Where will you go?" he asked. "You have no home here." "Nor anywhere," I answered. "But humans live on your world. You have bars?" His gaze was sobering. "You seek intoxicants?" I shrugged. "More than that. Solitude." I glanced at the human lieutenant, and back at the pedriquat. "Can you understand?" Commander Toarn stared at me for a long time before sighing. "You may go where you please. I understand." I sighed and rose to leave. The lieutenant escorted me as I walked, shakily, to the front door; and then he saw me out into the misty-skied world of the pedriquats, and I walked alone down the road toward the city, along the edge of the spaceport—a lonely cultural hero, wanting to forget. Wanting only to forget. ***** [Return to Table of Contents] OceanofPDF.com Alien Persuasion Behind the story: "Alien Persuasion" is where the Star Rigger Universe began—in my head, that is, not chronologically. It's the story of a rigger, a star pilot, someone who steers his ship by connecting to a sensory net and reaching out through something resembling virtual reality into the very stuff of space. (This hyperdimensional realm is called "flux-space" in this story and "the Flux" in the novels that followed.) The idea is that there exists a layer of multidimensional space that flows in streams like the luminiferous ether of Nineteenth Century physics, bypassing the tedious light-years between the stars.
